runs.text: Item, Modo de cortar em circulo.

lines.note: This is a Portuguese continuation from the preceding entry: “also, a way of cutting in a circle.” No Japanese form is printed on this physical line.
`Fanpan` gives ハンパン; `Fanpanna mono` gives ハンパンナ モノ and shows the adjectival construction. The Portuguese definition begins “a thing which…”.

runs.text: não està toda junta, & inteira como liuro que

lines.note: The definition says that the thing is not wholly assembled and complete, comparing it with a book; historical `liuro` is modern Portuguese `livro`.
This completes the example: a book “which lacks some part.” The tilde in `algũa` is retained diplomatically.
`Fanpû` gives ハンプゥ and is equated with `Xirami` シラミ. Portuguese `piolho` means a louse; the scan supports `û`, not the former `ǒ`.
`Fanqi` gives ハンキ. `Iyno vtçuuamono` is イイノ ウツワモノ, literally a vessel for cooked rice; Portuguese begins “a bowl, or…”.
This completes the gloss with roman Japanese `Goqi` ゴキ embedded in the Portuguese phrase `de arroz`, “for rice.”
`Fanqiǒjin` gives ハンキャゥジン, corresponding to 半狂人. Portuguese `meo doudo` is “half mad/a half-mad person.”

runs.text: Certo arco pequeno, ou bèſta de atirar.

lines.note: `Fanqiǔ` gives ハンキュゥ, naturally 半弓, a small bow. The long-`u` mark is visibly present in the scan; Portuguese also allows a small crossbow-like weapon.
`Fanqua` gives ハンクヮ. `Xiguei fana` is シゲイ ハナ, “dense/abundant flowers”; Portuguese begins “flowers or leaves very…”.

The Portuguese completes “very close together and dense.” Both `jũtas` and `baſtas` are scan-supported corrections of linguistically impossible OCR readings; `S.` is a printed source or register abbreviation.
`Fanriǔ` is ハンリュゥ and `Ichiriǔno fanbun` is イチリュゥノ ハンブン, “half of one grain.” Portuguese accordingly begins “half a grain of wheat…”.
This completes the Portuguese examples: a grain of wheat or rice. The physical hyphen joins `tri-` and `go` as `trigo`.
`Fanſan` gives ハンサン. `Sicazzoqi nacara` gives シカゾキ ナカラ and is glossed as half a drinking cup; the exact lexical identity of `Sicazzoqi` is less certain than the printed reading.
This completes the Portuguese gloss, “half a cup of wine.”

runs.text: Ferida feita como bustella, ou ſarna.

lines.note: `Fansǒ` gives ハンサゥ. Portuguese defines a wound resembling a pustule or scab; the scan has long `ſ` in `buſtella` and `ſarna`.
`Fanta` is ハンタ, naturally 繁多. `Xiguequ vouoi` gives シゲク オヲイ, “numerous in abundance”; Portuguese begins “many affairs or…”.
Portuguese completes “many occupations.” The Japanese example begins `Gofanta naredo-`, ゴハンタ ナレド…, “although you are very busy…”, with a printed line-end hyphen.

runs.text: Ainda que tenhais muito que fazer to-

lines.note: Initial `mo` completes `naredomo`. Portuguese gives the concessive sense, “although you have much to do…”. `Ainda`, formerly misread as `Aindi`, is clear from both language and scan.
Portuguese `toda via` completes “nevertheless.” The terminal `X.` is a printed abbreviation whose precise reference is not expanded in Level 1.
`Fanten` gives ハンテン and `Nacazora` ナカゾラ, literally the middle sky. Portuguese defines the middle region of the air.
`Fantǒ` gives ハンタゥ, naturally 半途; alternative `tochǔ` is トチュゥ, 途中. The scan supports both corrected long-vowel marks.
Portuguese completes “halfway, or on the road.” A second visible `Ou` is displaced at the far right; Level 1 records its physical placement without assigning it to a reconstructed logical entry.
`Fanuqedori` is ハヌケドリ, literally a bird lacking feathers. Portuguese begins “a bird without the feathers of its wings”; the scan reads `Paſſaro`, not the former `Puſſaro`.
The gloss adds “without wings.” Both words retain the printed long `ſ`.

runs.text: Mea caixa, que he a metade de hũa

lines.note: `Fanxen` gives ハンセン. Portuguese defines half a `caixa`, then explains it relative to a low-value copper coin.
This completes the monetary definition: “a low [denomination] copper coin.”
`Fanxen` is ハンセン, naturally 帆船; `Focaqebune` is ホカケブネ, 帆掛け船. Portuguese identifies a sailing vessel.
The example `Fãxen cajeni macaſuru` gives ハンセン カゼニ マカスル, “entrust the sailing vessel to the wind.” `macaſuru` is linguistically and visually supported over the former `maraſuru`.

runs.text: ção que vai à vella entregaſe ao vento.

lines.note: Portuguese translates the example: “the vessel which goes under sail gives itself over to the wind.” The scan reads `vai`, correcting `vui`.
`Fanxi` gives ハンシ, 半死, and `Nacarajini` gives ナカラジニ, “half dead.” Portuguese begins to explain its combination with another expression.
The line says that with `Fãjǒ` one says `Fanji fanjǒ`, ハンジ ハンジャゥ, the expression 半死半生. The earlier OCR sequence was semantically incoherent; the corrected reading is visible in the scan.
This second `Fanxi` is also ハンシ but has a different sense: a letter signed while otherwise blank. `Item` introduces another regional or documentary use.
The Portuguese locates the usage in `Chùgocu` チュウゴク and describes paper on which the `Yacata` writes. Both Japanese terms are roman type within the Portuguese explanation.
This completes the definition with `cartas`, “letters.”
`Fanxǔ` gives ハンシュゥ and is explained by `Focaqe bune` ホカケ ブネ, a sailing vessel. The scan clearly has final `xǔ`; the former `Fanxi` duplicated the preceding headword incorrectly.

runs.text: Hum paſſaro como coruo que tem

lines.note: `Fanxucqe` gives ハンシュッケ. Portuguese begins to identify a bird resembling a crow; the internal `cq` is scan-supported and must not be normalized from the generated kana.

runs.text: na cabeça hum ſinal branco como crista raſa.

lines.note: The bird has a white mark on its head like a low or flattened crest. Historical Portuguese spelling and long `ſ` are retained.
`Fanya` is ハンヤ, 半夜, and `Yonaca` ヨナカ, 夜中. The former `ranya. Tonaca` was an OCR failure contradicted by both the lexical pair and the scan.

runs.text: deas que durão ate mea noite.

lines.note: The additional sense concerns candles that last until midnight. The scan reads `durão`, not `dunão`; `Cã-` plus `deas` forms `Cãdeas` across the line break.
`Fanyei` gives ハンエイ, naturally 繁栄. `Xigueri ſacayuru` is シゲリ サカユル, “flourish and prosper,” matching Portuguese `Florecer`.
This completes `proſperar` and extends the sense to a family increasing or multiplying. No normalization of `multiplicarſe` or `algũa` is made in Level 1.
`Fanza` is ハンザ, 半座; `Zano fanbun` is ザノ ハンブン, “half of the sitting space/room.” The scan has capital `Z`, correcting the lowercase OCR form.
Portuguese completes “half a room or chamber.” `Fanzauo vaqete fitouo iſu` gives ハンザヲ ワケテ ヒトヲ イス, describing dividing the room and seating someone.

runs.text: S. Fazer aſſentar a alguem, dandolhe

lines.note: The scan begins with a distinct printed `S.` before the Portuguese explanation, not a stray period. The definition is “to make someone sit, giving him…”.
This completes “half a `Zaxiqi`,” with roman Japanese `Zaxiqi` ザシキ embedded in the Portuguese gloss. Its printed capital is preserved.
`Fanzacu` gives ハンザク, naturally 半作; `Nacara tçucuru` is ナカラ ツクル, “make incompletely.” The lost initial `F` in the OCR is unambiguous in the scan.
Portuguese completes the definition: “a half-made or imperfect work.”
`Fanzô` gives ハンゾゥ and denotes half a vessel or shipload. The example starts `Niga fan-`, with the word divided physically across the line.

runs.text: O fato he pera carregar meo nauio.

lines.note: Initial `zô` completes `fanzô`; `Niga fanzô aru` gives ニガ ハンゾゥ アル. Portuguese explains that the load is enough to fill half a ship.

runs.text: Hum vaſo de pao vruxado com que

lines.note: `Fanzǒ` gives ハンザゥ and is a distinct headword from `Fanzô`. Portuguese begins “a lacquered wooden vessel with which…”.
The vessel is used to pour water onto the hands. Historical `agoa` corresponds to modern Portuguese `água`.
`Fanzocu` is ハンゾク, 半俗; `Nacara zocu` is ナカラ ゾク, “half secular.” Portuguese contrasts half secular and half religious status.
The Portuguese completes “half religious” and introduces `Fanzocuni xite yefatuo…`, ハンゾクニ シテ エハツヲ…, as an example.

runs.text: Sendo meo ſecular he çujar o trajo

lines.note: `qegaſu` completes ケガス, so the example says that, being half secular, one defiles the religious habit or transmission. The Portuguese uses historical `çujar`.
This completes the phrase `trajo de religioſo`, “religious clothing/habit.”
This homonymous `Fanzocu` is ハンゾク in the sense “half a bundle.” `Iſſocuno fanbun` gives イッソクノ ハンブン, literally half of one bundle.

runs.text: de lenha, ou mea reſma de papel, &c.

lines.note: Portuguese gives examples: half a bundle of firewood or half a ream of paper. The printed nasal mark in `pãpel` is preserved.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de ſe eſpalhar algũa

lines.note: `Fappato` gives ハッパト and is explicitly adverbial. Portuguese begins “the manner in which something spreads”; the faint `l` in `eſpalhar` is recoverable from the scan and context.
The example is something spreading like a smell. The line is entirely Portuguese continuation.
`Fappi` gives ハッピ, modern 法被/半被. Portuguese defines garments used in an `auto`; the scan reads `ſeruem`, correcting the nonsensical OCR `ſerutem`.
`Fappiacu` is ハッピャク, 八百, “eight hundred,” exactly matching Portuguese `Oito centos`.
`Fappǒ` gives ハッパゥ, 八方; `Yatçuno cata` is ヤツノ カタ, “eight directions/sides.” Portuguese `Oito partes` confirms the reading and restores the missing `t` in `Oito`.
`Fappu` gives ハップ, naturally 髪膚. `Camigue, fadaye` is カミゲ、ハダエ, hair and skin/flesh; Portuguese begins with the hair of the head.

runs.text: beça, & carão, ou ſuperficie da carne.

lines.note: This completes `cabeça` and adds the skin or surface of the flesh. The precise historical sense of printed `carão` is less secure than the overall equation with `fadaye`.

runs.text: Dia em que ventão os oito ven-

lines.note: `Fappunichi` gives ハップニチ, a calendrical day associated with the eight winds. Portuguese begins “a day on which the eight winds blow…”.

runs.text: tos. i, Dia aziago no qual não ſe embarcão

lines.note: This completes `ventos` and explains the day as unlucky, one on which people do not embark. Printed `i,` introduces the explanatory equivalent.
The subject of `não ſe embarcão` is `os gentios`, the contemporary missionary term for non-Christians.

runs.text: Pincel largo pera eſtender o grude no

lines.note: `Faqe` gives ハケ, 刷毛, a broad brush. Portuguese first describes using it to spread paste on paper.

runs.text: papel, ou com que vruxão, cayão, &c.

lines.note: The gloss adds other brush uses, including lacquering and whitewashing. The unusual historical verbs are retained as printed rather than modernized in the transcription.
`Faqi` gives ハキ. `Yabureta vtçuuamono` is ヤブレタ ウツワモノ, “a broken vessel/container,” matching Portuguese `Vaſo…`.
This completes the Portuguese gloss, “broken vessel.”
`Faqi, qu, aita` records the inflectional forms of `faqu` ハク, here “to sweep.” The comma before the Portuguese gloss is preserved.
The same printed paradigm introduces `faqu` ハク, “to vomit.” `Chiuo faqu` is チヲ ハク, literally “vomit blood.”
Portuguese explains “to cast blood from the mouth.” The next Japanese example starts `Tçuuo fa-`, ツヲ ハ…, divided at the physical line end.
Initial `qu` completes `faqu`; `Tçuuo faqu` is ツヲ ハク, “to spit.” A further expression begins `Goncu, l, cuuo fa-`, with `l` meaning Latin *vel*, “or.”
`Goncu, l, cuuo faqu` gives ゴンク／クヲ ハク, “utter sayings/maxims,” reflected in Portuguese `Dizer ſentenças`. `Quǒguenuo fa-` starts a new example.
`Quǒguenuo faqu` gives クヮゥゲンヲ ハク, “utter boastful words.” Portuguese glosses this as saying boasts or swaggering threats.
This paradigm is `faqu` ハク in the distinct sense “to put on footwear.” `Tabiuo faqu` is タビヲ ハク, to put on `Tabi`.
Portuguese translates the `Tabi` example, then gives `Tachiuo faqu`, タチヲ ハク, literally to wear or gird on a long sword.
This completes `Cingir montante`, “to gird on a long sword.” The physical hyphen joins `Cin-` and `gir`.
`Faqiacu` gives ハキャク, naturally 破却; `Yaburu` is ヤブル, “destroy/break.” The former OCR `Ynburu` fails both the Japanese morphology and the scan.
`Faqiague, uru, eta` records ハキアゲル and its inflectional forms. Portuguese describes stepping up while still shod, for example onto a raised room or veranda.
This completes the locations with `zaxiqi` ザシキ and a veranda. Here `zaxiqi` is printed in the same italic run as the Portuguese continuation, so Level 1 preserves that typography.
`Faqicaqe, uru, eta` gives ハキカケル, “to spit upon.” Portuguese states the same sense directly; printed long `ſ` and the tilde in `algũa` are retained.
A proverb-like example begins `Fitono vyeuo vttayuru monoua`, ヒトノ ウエヲ ウッタユル モノワ, “one who accuses another…”. `chi-` begins “blood” across the line break.

Initial `uo` completes `chiuo`, チヲ. The clause continues `fucunde fitoni faqicaquruto vonaji`, “is like holding blood in the mouth and spitting it on another”; enlargement shows plain `uo`, not OCR-derived `uǒ`.

runs.text: O que acuſa a outros, he co-

lines.note: `cotogia` completes the Japanese as コトヂャ, “it is the same thing.” `Fab.` introduces the Portuguese explanation: “one who accuses others is like…”.

runs.text: mo o que com a boca chea de ſangue cospe em

lines.note: Portuguese continues the comparison with someone who, with a mouth full of blood, spits on another person.

runs.text: outro ficãdo elle tambẽ çujo, e enſangoentado.

lines.note: The accuser likewise remains dirty and bloodstained. The scan reads conjunction `e`, correcting OCR `c`; the nasal marks in `ficãdo` and `tambẽ` are preserved where printed.
`Faqichiraxi, ſu, aita` gives ハキチラシ／ハキチラス, “scatter by sweeping.” Portuguese `Varrendo eſpalhar` is an exact compositional gloss.
`Faqidaxi, ſu, aita` gives ハキダシ／ハキダス. Portuguese supplies both senses, “spit out” and “sweep out.”
This completes the second Portuguese sense: to sweep outward. Historical `pera` is retained rather than modernized to `para`.
`Faqifarai, ǒ, ǒta` gives ハキハライ／ハキハラウ, “sweep away.” The initial `F` lost by OCR is clear in the scan and agrees with the entry sequence.
Portuguese completes the definition, “to throw out by sweeping.”
